title: Elastic Moduli
short_intro: Elastic moduli are material constants that quantify the linear relationship between stress and strain within the elastic limit. They characterize the resistance of a solid body to deformation under applied external forces.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Definition of stress, strain, Hooke's law, Young's modulus (Y), Bulk modulus (K), Modulus of rigidity (eta), and Poisson's ratio (sigma).
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Interrelations between elastic constants (Y, K, eta, sigma), strain energy density, twisting of a cylinder, and bending of beams.

prerequisites: Newton's laws of motion and static equilibrium
Concept of internal restoring forces and intermolecular bonding
Basic tensor and directional properties of stress and strain

concept_notes.heading: Stress and Strain Fundamentals
bullets: Stress is defined as the internal restoring force per unit area, measured in N/m<sup>2</sup> or Pascal.
Longitudinal stress produces a change in length, shearing stress changes shape, and volumetric (hydraulic) stress changes volume.
Strain is a dimensionless quantity representing the fractional deformation produced in the body.

concept_notes.heading: Hooke's Law and Elastic Moduli
bullets: Within the elastic limit, stress is directly proportional to strain, defining the generalized Hooke's law.
Young's modulus (Y) governs longitudinal deformation, bulk modulus (K) governs volumetric compression, and rigidity modulus (eta) governs shape distortion.
The reciprocal of bulk modulus is known as compressibility.

concept_notes.heading: Poisson's Ratio
bullets: Poisson's ratio (sigma) is the ratio of lateral strain to longitudinal strain under uniaxial stress.
For isotropic elastic materials, the theoretical limits of Poisson's ratio are -1 to 0.5.
Most common engineering materials exhibit a positive Poisson's ratio between 0.25 and 0.35.

concept_notes.heading: Interrelations Between Elastic Constants
bullets: Four elastic constants (Y, K, eta, sigma) are used to describe isotropic elasticity, of which only two are independent.
Standard relations include Y = 3K(1 - 2sigma) and Y = 2eta(1 + sigma).
Eliminating sigma yields the master relation between Y, K, and eta: Y = (9Keta) / (3K + eta).

derivations.title: Work Done in Stretching a Wire (Strain Energy)
derivations.conditions: Isotropic wire of length L and cross-sectional area A obeying Hooke's law
steps: Let the instantaneous extension of the wire be x under a stretching force F.
According to Hooke's law, F = (Y A / L) x.
The small work done dW in producing an additional extension dx is given by dW = F dx = (Y A / L) x dx.
Integrating from x = 0 to x = delta L gives total work W = int_{0}^{\Delta L} \frac{YA}{L} x \, dx = \frac{YA (\Delta L)^2}{2L}.
Rewriting in terms of stress and strain gives Work = (1/2) * Stress * Strain * Volume.

derivations.title: Relation between Y, K, and sigma
derivations.conditions: Isotropic material subjected to uniform triaxial tensile stress
steps: Consider a cube of side l subjected to equal tensile stresses P along three mutually perpendicular directions X, Y, and Z.
The longitudinal strain along X due to stress along X is P/Y, and the lateral strains due to stresses along Y and Z are -sigma(P/Y) each.
Total net longitudinal strain along any edge is epsilon = \frac{P}{Y} - \sigma\frac{P}{Y} - \sigma\frac{P}{Y} = \frac{P}{Y}(1 - 2\sigma).
The volumetric strain is Delta V / V = 3 * epsilon = \frac{3P}{Y}(1 - 2\sigma).
By definition of bulk modulus, K = P / (Delta V / V) = \frac{P}{3P(1 - 2\sigma) / Y} = \frac{Y}{3(1 - 2\sigma)}.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Stress-Strain Curve for a Ductile Metal
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A curve plotting tensile stress on the y-axis against engineering strain on the x-axis, highlighting the proportional limit, yield point, ultimate tensile strength point, and fracture point.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The initial linear region follows Hooke's law where slope equals Young's modulus. Beyond the yield point, permanent plastic deformation occurs.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Frequently tested for identifying elastic limit, yield strength, and toughness (area under the curve).

graphs_and_experiments.title: Searle's Apparatus Experiment
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Schematic setup showing two identical wires suspended from a rigid support, with a spirit level, micrometer screw gauge, and dead load pan.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Used to experimentally determine Young's modulus of a material in wire form by measuring microscopic extensions accurately.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Conceptual questions on experimental error minimization and least count of the micrometer screw.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Bending of Beams (Elastic Depression)
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A loaded beam supported at both ends showing central sag (depression) delta.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Depression delta is inversely proportional to Young's modulus Y and geometrical moment of inertia.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Questions on how beam geometry (rectangular vs circular cross-section) affects structural rigidity.

solved_numericals.question: A steel wire of length 2 m and cross-sectional area 1 mm<sup>2</sup> is stretched by 2 mm. If Young's modulus of steel is 2 * 10<sup>11</sup> N/m<sup>2</sup>, calculate the tension developed in the wire.
solution_steps: Identify given parameters: L = 2 m, A = 1 mm<sup>2</sup> = 1 * 10<sup>-6</sup> m<sup>2</sup>, Delta L = 2 mm = 2 * 10<sup>-3</sup> m, Y = 2 * 10<sup>11</sup> N/m<sup>2</sup>.
Use formula: F = (Y * A * Delta L) / L.

solved_numericals.question: For a given material, the Young's modulus is 1.2 * 10<sup>11</sup> N/m<sup>2</sup> and the Poisson's ratio is 0.25. Calculate its bulk modulus and modulus of rigidity.
solution_steps: Use formula relating Y, K, and sigma: Y = 3K(1 - 2sigma).
Use formula relating Y, eta, and sigma: Y = 2eta(1 + sigma).
solved_numericals.answer: Bulk Modulus = 8 * 10<sup>10</sup> N/m<sup>2</sup>, Rigidity Modulus = 4.8 * 10<sup>10</sup> N/m<sup>2</sup>

solved_numericals.question: Find the fractional change in volume of a glass slab of bulk modulus 3.7 * 10<sup>10</sup> N/m<sup>2</sup> when subjected to a hydraulic pressure of 10<sup>7</sup> N/m<sup>2</sup>.
solution_steps: Given K = 3.7 * 10<sup>10</sup> N/m<sup>2</sup> and P = 10<sup>7</sup> N/m<sup>2</sup>.
Use bulk modulus relation: K = - P / (Delta V / V).
Rearrange for fractional volume change: Delta V / V = - P / K.

assumptions_and_limitations: Hooke's law is assumed to hold strictly, which is only valid within the proportional elastic limit of the material.
Materials are assumed to be perfectly isotropic, homogeneous, and continuous, neglecting crystalline grain boundaries and microscopic defects.

common_misconceptions.wrong: A material with a higher Young's modulus is always stronger and harder to break.
common_misconceptions.correct: Young's modulus measures elastic stiffness (resistance to deformation), whereas breaking strength refers to the ultimate tensile stress before fracture.
common_misconceptions.why: A material can be very stiff (high Y) yet brittle, failing at a low ultimate strain.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Poisson's ratio can take any positive value.
common_misconceptions.correct: Thermodynamic stability and strain energy constraints limit Poisson's ratio for isotropic solids between -1.0 and 0.5.
common_misconceptions.why: If sigma exceeded 0.5, the bulk modulus or rigidity modulus would become negative, violating mechanical stability.

quick_revision: Young's modulus governs length changes, bulk modulus governs volume changes, and rigidity modulus governs shape changes under shear.
